en: The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai says in the ninth fascicle:
"The Buddha-nature of ordinary beings is like a newborn calf, whose blood and milk have not yet been distinguished.
The Buddha-nature of *śrāvakas* is like pure milk. That of *pratyekabuddhas* is like curd. That of *bodhisattvas* is like [the stages of] raw and cooked [milk]."
"Sū, the Buddha is like the finest cream (mṛdvīkā).
This analogy refers to the five stages of the Separate Teaching (pratyeka-śāsana).
Milk is a metaphor for ignorance, and blood is a metaphor for the four abodes [of afflictions].
Ordinary beings possess these, and thus it is said they are "mixed with blood.
Those in the ten stages have already severed the blood of the four abodes and are equal to the two vehicles; therefore, it is said that śrāvakas are like milk.
In the final mind of the Ten Abidings, one’s principle is clear and wisdom is sharp; because one has begun to erode the habitual tendencies of a Pratyekabuddha, it is said to be like curd.
In the Ten Practices, one destroys the "dust-sands" [of afflictions], which is like fresh ghee (*sarpis*).
The ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) shatter the dust and sand of the realms beyond, like refined butter (*sarpis*).
Therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva is like raw or refined butter.

Upon ascending the stages (*bhūmi*), one shatters ignorance (*avidyā*), manifests the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), attains the single body and the infinite bodies, and performs the eight manifestations of Buddhahood within a hundred Buddha-worlds; therefore, it is said that a Buddha is like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Twenty-fifth, it says:
"On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Patience.
If a cow eats it, she immediately obtains the *amṛta* (clarified butter)."
"The ox represents the ordinary person, and the grass represents the Eightfold Noble Path.
One who is able to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path perceives the Buddha-nature; this is called attaining the *amṛta* (clarified butter).

This is an analogy for the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), which follows the great direct path and observes all sentient beings as being, in their very nature, *nirvāṇa*, such that they can no longer be extinguished."
Perfect faith and perfect practice do not proceed through gradual stages; within a single lifetime, one immediately enters the first stage (the First Abode) and attains the vision of Buddha-nature.

This is like a cow eating the "patience-grass" (kṣānti-tṛṇa), which bypasses the four intermediate flavors and directly yields the finest essence, *amṛta* (ghee). Thus, one should know that this is the purport of the Perfect Teaching (*vaidalya-yāna*).

The "sacrificial grass" (kṣānti-tṛṇa) is a metaphor for the excellence of the object; the "cow" is a metaphor for the excellence of wisdom; the "eater" is a metaphor for the excellence of practice; and the production of "ghee" (ghṛta) is a metaphor for the excellence of the stages—this is the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].
When the cow eats other grass, its blood and milk undergo transformation; only after passing through the four flavors does it finally become ghee.
The other provisional teachings regarding the object, wisdom, practice, and stages are all coarse in intent.
As for the preceding four analogies, they clarify the *amṛta* (clarified butter) in four distinct locations.
The four teachings clarify that the Buddha-wisdoms differ from one another; yet since all are called "Buddha," they equally point to Buddha-wisdom as being the *amṛta* (the finest essence).

In the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka) and *Shared* (Sādhāraṇa) vehicles, the two types of Buddhas do not clarify the Middle Way; rather, they take the wisdom of the two truths of the fruit-stage Buddha as the *amṛta*.

In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), upon ascending to the stages (bhūmi) and shattering ignorance, one is immediately able to become a Buddha; thus, the wisdom of the Middle Way is termed *amṛta* (the finest essence).
In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the wisdom of the Middle Way is attained at the first dwelling (prathama-vihāra), which is likewise called *amṛta*.
The *Sūryagarbha-alaṃkāra* states:
"The World-Honored One’s sudden awakening" refers to the wisdom of this first stage (*bhūmi*), which constitutes the *amṛta* (the finest essence).
The two preceding forms of *amṛta* are provisional and not ultimate; therefore, while there are teachings, there is no person [who realizes them].
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the *amṛta* (tíhú) is termed "expedient in principle but real in fact"; in the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào), the *amṛta* is termed "real in both principle and fact.
For this reason, the three preceding stages and the five flavors are all coarse, whereas the single flavor of the Perfect Teaching is entirely subtle.
The twenty-seventh fascicle states:
"For example, if someone places poison in milk, it can kill a person;
even when it has reached the stage of clarified butter (ghṛta), it can still kill a person."
This analogy serves two purposes:
first, it applies generally to both the gradual and sudden approaches to clarify that the teachings are indeterminate, showing that the Buddha-nature can be perceived everywhere;
second, it pertains to the indeterminacy of practice.
The mental activities of one who practices are like milk;
the wisdom of the true nature is likened to poison. Just as poison has the power to take life, this wisdom possesses the power to destroy ignorance.

Since time immemorial, the poison of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) has been spoken of; it is placed within the milk of the ordinary person’s mind. When the poisonous wisdom unfolds, it cannot be fixed as to when it will manifest—whether it arises from the first flavor or the final flavor—and thus its sequence cannot be definitively determined. Therefore, it is said that the poison is placed within the milk, and so on, through to the clarified butter (*ghṛta*); it pervades all five flavors, and in each, there is the potential for death.

If sentient beings, starting from the stage of ordinary people, were to hear the *Avataṃsaka* and immediately perceive the principle and enter the Buddha’s wisdom, this would be like killing someone with blood or milk.
If one had previously attained the Ten Abodes and now attains awakening through the *Avataṃsaka*, this is like killing someone with the curd within the cream-of-milk.
One who awakens through the Ten Practices is like killing someone with the fresh butter within the cream-of-milk.
Those who attain awakening through the Ten Dedications are "killed" within the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Those who further awaken through the various stages (*bhūmi*) are "killed" within the *maṇḍa* (the finest essence).

If it concerns the past, those who previously held the provisional names and semblance stages within the Perfect Teaching and now attain awakening upon hearing the *Avataṃsaka*, are likewise "killed" within the milk, and are also "killed" within the curd, fresh butter, and clarified butter.

If one was previously in stages such as the various abodes (*vihāra*) and practices (*caryā*), yet now hears the *Avataṃsaka* and thereby increases the Path while diminishing rebirth, this is like killing someone within the finest ghee (*sarpirmaṇḍa*). So it is said.

If, within the teachings of the Tripitaka, ordinary beings and those in the stage of skillful means, as well as bodhisattvas, hear the Tripitaka teachings and are thereby able to secretly perceive the Middle Way therein, this is like killing a person with milk.
If, within the stages of the four fruits, one secretly perceives the Middle Way, this is like killing someone within the curd.
In the explicit teachings, such a thing does not exist.

If, within the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), ordinary beings or those in the preparatory stages of the Three Vehicles hear the Shared Teaching and secretly perceive the Buddha-nature, this is like killing someone within the milk.
If one who has entered the stages departs in secret, this is like killing a person within curdled milk (*dadhi*).
If one departs while within the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgajñatā*), this is like killing a person within fresh butter (*navanīta*).
In the ninth stage, it is like killing a person with matured butter (*ghṛta*).
In the tenth stage, it is like killing a person within the finest essence (*sarpis*).
For the Śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), there is only "killing by secret means," but no "killing by manifest or indeterminate means."
If, within the context of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one departs after hearing the teaching during the stage of the ten faiths (shixin), this is like killing someone with milk.
If one departs during the thirty minds (sanshixin), this is like killing someone with curd (yili). It is also like killing someone with fresh or processed butter (shengsu/shushu).
To ascend to the stage [of *amṛta*] and then depart is to kill the person within the *ghṛta*.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), for one to immediately shatter ignorance and perceive the Buddha-nature upon first hearing the sutra is to kill the person within the milk.
When the six sense organs have become pure, this is like the fresh butter (*navanīta*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that kill people.
If one has reached the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), this is like the supreme cream (*sarpis*) that kills people.

If there is a practitioner who, having passed through the four teachings and the five flavors, only then enters the supreme cream of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) and kills people, this is the "breaking of the three to reveal the one," where the relative comparison of these stages constitutes their subtlety.

If poison were placed within milk such that every single taste would kill a person, this is the opening of the provisional to reveal the real, whereby one perceives the Middle Way within all phenomena.
Therefore, the text says:
"That which you practice is the path of the bodhisattva.
There is no need to change one's route or alter one's tracks to seek the truth; the sublime is seen within the coarse. Thus, the analogy of placing poison [in food] is employed.

All sutras possess the subtle art of placing poison in secret; yet none have yet revealed this through a gradual tasting that leads into the sublime, nor have they explicitly resolved the coarse to reveal the sublime.
It is only upon reaching this point in the *Lotus Sūtra* that two meanings emerge.

All beings ride together on the precious vehicle and all open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; as these matters are now fully revealed and manifest, it alone is called "Wondrous. This is the intended meaning.
Entering the sublime through sequence and opening the coarse to reveal the sublime each have two meanings:
entering by conforming to the stages (*anupūrvika*) and entering through progressive advancement (*viśeṣagamana*).

If it is said that the definitive teaching of the Śrāvaka-dharma is the king of all sutras, and that upon hearing it and reflecting on it with discernment, one draws near to the unsurpassed path—this refers to revealing the sublime by conforming to the stages.
Increasing the Path and diminishing Birth is precisely ascending into the Sublime;
therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* alone designates it as "Sublime.

Tenth, clarifying the beginning and end of the sublime stages: within the Dharma of True Suchness, there is no sequential progression, nor are there first or second stages. Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal and eternally quiescent, how could one differentiate between beginning, end, or start and finish?

This is truly because, through the great wisdom of equality, one contemplates that the dharma-realm has no diversity; thus, one is able to shatter the various forms of ignorance and manifest the wisdom that is free from diversity.
Based on this wisdom, that which has no beginning yet begins is the initial *A*;
that which has no end yet ends is the final *Cha*;
and that which has no middle yet is discussed as having a middle constitutes the forty minds (*cittas*).
Although there are distinctions, there is in fact no distinction; therefore, it is called the "Inconceivable Stage.
As the subsequent text states:

"Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are like a grove of bamboo; those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and those who are non-retrogressive, and so forth, are all unable to know it, except for those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and stable."

"That which cannot be known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" distinguishes [this teaching] from the two types of *dviyāna* practitioners—the Śrāvakas and those of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

As for the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, they do not even reach the level of the Śrāvakas regarding the contemplation of reality; if the Śrāvakas themselves do not know it, how could these Bodhisattvas possibly know it?
The wisdom with which Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching enter into truth is no different from that of the Two Vehicles; what the Two Vehicles do not know, those Bodhisattvas likewise do not know.
Now, by indicating that the Two Vehicles do not know it, it is shown that the Bodhisattvas at both stages cannot fathom it either.
"Being unaware when the mind is first aroused" refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-śāsana*);
"being unable to know [the state of] non-retrogression" refers to the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) of the Distinct Teaching.
In the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), there is non-retrogression in terms of position (*sthāna*).
In the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*), there is non-retrogression in action;
in the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), there is non-retrogression in mindfulness.
These three types of non-retrogression cannot be known [by others].
If one does not regress within the Tripiṭaka teaching, one still does not equal the Two Vehicles;

if one does not regress within the Shared Teaching, one merely equals the Two Vehicles. Since the Two Vehicles do not even know [of such non-regression], how could they possibly be mentioned again as Bodhisattvas?
Now, those who mark themselves as having attained non-retrogression in their resolve correspond to the practitioners of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
"Power of faith" refers to the stage of provisional names;
"firmness" refers to the stage of the Iron Wheel.
In such stages as these, one attains understanding upon hearing the sutra; thus they are considered "wondrous," representing the beginning of the semblance stage (*sadr̥śabhūmi*).
The initial opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, wherein one mounts this precious vehicle and travels toward the eastern direction, marks the beginning of the true stage (*bhūtasthāna*).
The three stages are the middle positions, extending all the way to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); beyond this, there is no word to be spoken, which constitutes the ultimate position.
By what vehicle do these various positions ride?
There are three kinds of vehicles:
namely, the vehicle of teaching, the vehicle of practice, and the vehicle of realization.
If one speaks of this vehicle, it departs from the triple world and arrives at abiding within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
There are two meanings of "abiding":
first, abiding by means of attaining realization, which refers to the intent of the Shared Teaching;
second, abiding because that which is mounted is ultimate, which refers to the intent of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.
The beginner relies on the teachings as they are expounded; by believing the teachings and establishing practice, one escapes the three realms.
Because ignorance has not yet been shattered and nothing has yet been realized, one does not see the Truth.
"I have merely come here by means of the Vehicle of Teaching.
Within my Perfect Teaching, who is it that corresponds?

It refers to the disciples of the five grades who are able to skillfully give rise to the Great Mind; they are the ones who have forever parted from the ocean of suffering in the wheel of the triple world."

When the vehicle of teaching has ceased and the vehicle of realization has not yet been reached, one cultivates various practices with the wisdom of semblance-understanding; thus, taking practice as the vehicle, one emerges from the triple world of expedient means and arrives at the abiding within the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) of the first stage.
Within my Perfect Teaching (Eka-yāna), who is it that [attains this]?
It refers to those with the ten levels of faith whose six sense faculties have become pure; such are the ones.

From the first stage (Prathamabhūmi) up to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), those who further increase their Path and diminish their births take realization as their vehicle. Emerging from the three realms of causes and conditions through to the three realms of no-more-birth, they arrive at Sublime Enlightenment (Miao-jue). There, beyond the characters "cha" and "wu," there is nothing more that can be said; therefore, it is called "abiding within Sarvajñā (Omniscience)."
The various vehicles that preceded this still possessed higher dharmas beyond them, and thus could not be called "abiding.
Here, there is no dharma superior to it; for this reason, it is said to be "abiding.
To abide in the place of non-abiding is precisely the culmination of the wondrous stage.

Furthermore, in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Ten Abidings (shizhu) destroy the afflictions of views and thought (jian-si), which constitutes traveling three hundred *yojanas*; the Ten Practices (shixing) destroy the afflictions of dust and sand (chen-sha), constituting four hundred; and the Ten Dedications (shihuixiang) subdue ignorance (wuming), constituting five hundred.
The Tenth Ground severs ignorance; this stage is the partial realization of the Middle Way and constitutes the place of treasure.
In the Perfect Teaching, the time when the six sense organs are purified corresponds to the fourth hundred [of the ten stages].
Breaking through ignorance to enter the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) constitutes the five hundred [yojanas] of practice.

When those of the two vehicles hear this sutra, they break through the delusions of ignorance, open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and receive the prediction of Buddhahood; this is precisely the definitive resolution of all coarse stages, having passed the five hundred yojanas to enter the first stage.
This is the beginning of the stage of wondrousness; having attained the vehicle of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-yāna*), one travels to the East.

When one reaches the "increase of the path and decrease of birth" within the Fundamental Gate, one further mounts the vehicle of realization and travels to the South; this is the entry into the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*).
The west represents entering the ten stages of dedication (daśa-pratipatti).
The north represents entering the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi).
Furthermore, as the text says:

"When it was said that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is long and far-reaching, six hundred and eighty trillion nayutas of people, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)"; this refers to the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
"Furthermore, a thousandfold more bodhisattvas attain the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining," which refers to the ten practices (*daśapratipatti*).
"Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a world-system who attain the eloquence of joyful speech," which refers to the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).
"Furthermore, there are as many as the atoms in a world who have attained the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*," which refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*).
"There are as many as the atoms in a trichiliocosm who have attained non-retrogression," which refers to the second stage.
"By means of the atoms of two thousand lands, one is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma," refers to the third stage (bhūmi).
"By means of the atoms of a small chiliocosm, one shall attain bodhi after eight births," refers to the fourth stage.
To attain it within seven births corresponds to the fifth stage (bhūmi).
To attain it within six births corresponds to the sixth stage.
To attain it within five births corresponds to the seventh stage.
"To be attained in four births" refers to the eighth stage;
"to be attained in three births" refers to the ninth stage; and "to be attained in two births" refers to the tenth stage.
"One shall attain in one lifetime" refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).
Once this single lifetime has passed—corresponding to the passing of the character "Cha"—one reaches the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Suyojana), which is the culmination of the sublime positions.
To cite the text of the *Lotus Sūtra* from the preceding section on the stages and incorporate it here to form a single topical division would not be cumbersome.
Fifth, regarding the "Excellence of the Three Dharmas," these are the dharmas in which the excellent stages abide.
The so-called "three dharmas" refer to the three *kṛti*s (guidelines).
The term *kṛti* means a model or standard; it is these three dharmas that serve as the models.
This consists of seven points:
I. A general explanation of the three modes of practice.
II. A detailed explanation of the three modes of practice. III.
A judgment on their coarseness and subtlety.
4. Revealing the coarse to manifest the subtle;
5. Clarifying the beginning and the end;
6. Categorizing according to the three dharmas.
Seven: A Critical Examination of the Siddhāntas.
First, a general explanation of the three tracks (*trayamārga*):
first, the track of true nature (*tathatāmārga*).
Second, the track of contemplative illumination;
third, the track of material support and accomplishment.
Although there are three names, they constitute nothing other than the Single Vehicle of the Mahāyāna.
The Sūtra says:
"If one seeks thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle.

This Single Buddha Vehicle is endowed with three dharmas: it is also called the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya), it is also called the Ultimate Emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā), and it is also called the Tathāgatagarbha.
These three indeterminate threes are three yet discussed as one;
this one indeterminate one is one yet discussed as three. It is inconceivable—neither unified nor distinct—the letter *I* and the celestial eye.
Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Buddha-nature is both one, not one, neither one nor not one.
It is 'one' because all sentient beings are of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*)."
"These words refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
'Not one' refers to the nature of numerical phenomena.
These words refer to the *tathāgatagarbha*."
"Neither one nor not-one; because the categories of numbered and unnumbered phenomena are not fixed.
This statement refers to the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The repeated use of the term "also" (*api*) is for the sake of emphasis.
It is but a single dharma, yet it is also called three;
therefore, it cannot be grasped as singular, nor can it be grasped as multiple. It is neither vertical nor horizontal, yet it is both three and one.

The preceding elucidation of the various truths—whether categorized as expanded or condensed, coarse or subtle, and so forth—constitutes the characteristics of the *tathatā-prakṛti-vidhi* (the track of the true nature).

The preceding elucidation of the various wisdoms—whether categorized as expanded or condensed, coarse or subtle—constitutes the characteristics of the *vipaśyanā-prakṛti-vidhi* (the track of contemplative observation).

The preceding clarification of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—whether categorized by their opening or closing, or by their coarseness or subtlety—constitutes the characteristics of the path for accomplishment.
The preceding clarification of the various stages is merely the fruit realized through the cultivation of these three dharmas.
If this is so, why is it explained again? There are three reasons for the repeated explanation:
first, the preceding objects, wisdoms, and practices constitute the three tracks traversed within the causal stage.
Now, it is clarified that this vehicle is the Mahāyāna; it has already reached the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and constitutes the three modes of abiding for the realization of the fruit.
Second, whereas previously the terms "object" (viṣaya) and "wisdom" (jñāna) were explained separately, here they are explained together under the name "Dharma."
Third, previously there was a direct and straightforward exposition that did not discuss the root and the branches.
Now, discussing the root from afar, it refers to the three tracks of inherent virtue, also called the Tathāgata-garbha;
discussing the branches to the ultimate degree, it refers to the three tracks of cultivated virtue, also called the Secret Treasury.
The root and the branches encompass all dharmas.
From the three dharmas of inherent virtue, the three dharmas of names and designations arise;
based on the three dharmas of names and designations, one cultivates the three dharmas of contemplative practice.
Based on the three dharmas of contemplative practice, the three corresponding dharmas are produced;
this continues up to the three dharmas of partial realization and the three dharmas of ultimate perfection.
Since these consist of the three dharmas for one's own benefit and the three dharmas for the benefit of others, it is appropriate that they be explained again for this reason.
I maintain that one phrase is itself three phrases, and three phrases are themselves one phrase; this is called the Perfect Buddha Vehicle (Yuanfo-cheng).
Since the *Ji* states that all expedient means emerge from the single phrase of the Tathāgata-garbha, this is a specific judgment; by analogy, it should be understood as a general opening.
It is "not one" because it is a numerical category of phenomena (*dharma*).
This is designated as the *tathāgatagarbha* to provide the expedient means (*upāya*) for unfolding the phenomena and characteristics of the three vehicles within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
It is neither one nor not one, because it is not fixed.

This single phrase is designated as the emptiness of the primary meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā), which opens up the three types of persons of the Shared Teaching (p’ung-hsiao) as being true within the very phenomena themselves.
Furthermore, it is "one" because all sentient beings are entirely of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
This single phrase is designated as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), from which the distinct teaching of the exclusive Bodhisattva vehicle is opened forth.
All these skillful means (upāya) emerge entirely from the Perfect [Teaching].
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Within the single Buddha-vehicle, I have distinguished and taught three.
This is precisely that meaning.

Second, regarding the detailed explanation of the three dharmas: one must first understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means of opening and closing [the teachings], and only then will one comprehend how these three dharmas are collectively subsumed into the One Great Vehicle.
From what dharmas does the Buddha open up the various provisional vehicles?
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that the Buddha-nature is not singular, yet teaches the three vehicles through such numerical categories of dharmas.
You should know that all the various vehicles and numerical dharmas are subsumed within the Tathāgatagarbha.
From this garbha, the Buddha has brought forth the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, including both their general and specific aspects.

Why is this? Since all vehicles are expedient means (*upāya*) and the *tathāgatagarbha* is the underlying reality (*vastu*), and since expedient means arise from that reality, it is said that all provisional teachings are subsumed within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Furthermore, based on the sūtras, the *Mahā-saṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The śrāvaka saṃgha is called the conditioned saṃgha. It also says:
"The adornment of merit through the six pāramitās.
It is also said:
"Because śrāvakas possess an abundance of concentration-power, they do not perceive the Buddha-nature."
"You should know that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is itself merit (*puṇya*), and merit is merely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* refers to it as 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*).
For example:"
Because views and thoughts within the realm have not yet been destroyed, there is activity and formation; thus they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Because their grasping is improper, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
Because they are not the dharma of wisdom, they are called "merit" (*puṇya*).
Now, looking upward from below, it should also be understood in this way:
the Two Vehicles have not yet destroyed the *pariṇāmi-śarīra* (the body of transformation), and thus they still belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
because they have not yet escaped ignorance (*avidyā*), they are said to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Because it is not the wisdom of the Middle Way, it is called "merit.

For this reason, one should know that the various vehicles of skillful means are all subsumed within the provisions for attainment; they all emerge from a single phrase of the Mahāyāna and are not the ultimate Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "Within the One Buddha Vehicle, [the Buddha] discriminately teaches three."
This is precisely that meaning.
It is also the case that within the single Buddha-vehicle (ekabuddhayāna), one distinguishes and teaches five;
and it is also the case that one distinguishes and teaches seven.
This is also explained through ninefold distinctions.
According to this interpretation, the phrase "Tathāgatagarbha" opens up various skillful means and the teachings of the provisional vehicles.

Next, regarding the discussion of the three dharmas for each of the four teachings in turn: within the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka-yāna), wisdom that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called the "principle of contemplative observation" (*vipaśyanā-naya*).
This constitutes the essence of the vehicle (*yāna*). The factors that assist the path and complete the vehicle are called the "principle of supportive accomplishment" (*sambhāra-naya*).
The primary and auxiliary vehicles involve severing delusions to enter the truth; this "truth" is the track of true nature (*tathatā*).
Since the teachings come to explain this, the teachings themselves are regarded as the vehicle.
The same applies to the Pratyekabuddhas. As for Bodhisattvas, they take the contemplation of impermanence as their mode of observation.
The nourishment of merit and virtue constitutes the "accomplishing" [vehicle];
sitting at the site of enlightenment, severing the fetters, and perceiving the truth constitutes the "true nature.

This teaching explicates the truth; by means of this vehicle of teaching, one emerges from the three realms and dwells within *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Since the verbal teaching has already been exhausted, there is no further vehicle of teaching.
Because the Truth cannot be operated upon, it is realized that it is not a vehicle; thus, there is the sense of seeking a vehicle, and so forth.
Second, the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) takes the track of true nature (zhenxing gui) as the essence of the vehicle.
Why is this so? Form itself is emptiness; within phenomena there is principle, and this principle is precisely the truth. Therefore, it constitutes the essence of the vehicle.
Taking the wisdom of emptiness as contemplative observation, one takes various practices as the supporting accomplishment.
This teaching elucidates the Truth; the vehicle is this vehicle of teaching. By departing from the triple world and arriving at the state of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one abides therein.

Once the Bodhisattva has departed from the triple world, they take practice as their vehicle to purify Buddha-fields and transform sentient beings, until finally reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), at which point they may truly be said to abide.
Furthermore, there is the teaching but no person;

there is no one who abides. This also signifies that the teaching has ceased and quiescence is realized, such that there is no further activity of meaning. It also implies the sense of seeking the vehicle, and so forth.

Third, regarding the clarification of the three dharmas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao): taking the contemplative observation of conditioned cultivation as the essence of the vehicle, with all practices serving as its supportive completion; these two dharmas together constitute the wisdom of conditioned cultivation.

Wisdom can destroy delusions and reveal principle, whereas principle cannot destroy delusions; if principle were able to destroy delusions, then since all sentient beings fully possess the nature of principle, why do they not destroy them?
If one attains this wisdom, one can then destroy delusions; therefore, wisdom is taken as the essence of the vehicle.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"That which is unconditioned and untainted is called the Bodhisattva Saṃgha."
"The wisdom of the first stage, the second stage, and so forth up to the tenth stage is called the 'Adornment of Wisdom.
Because this wisdom functions to traverse the ten stages, it constitutes the essence of the vehicle."
However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* elucidates three kinds of vehicles:
the vehicle of principle (*li-cheng*), the vehicle of conformity (*sui-cheng*), and the vehicle of attainment (*de-cheng*).
"Principle" refers to suchness prior to the path (*dao-qian zhenru*).
"Following" means that through the contemplation of suchness, wisdom accords with its object.
"Attaining" means that the habitual perfuming of all practices and vows perfumes non-conceptual wisdom, which then accords with the non-conceptual object and enters into resonance with suchness.
These three meanings are, at first glance, similar to the three tracks (*triyāna*), yet they have not yet been fully integrated.

Why is this? The ninth consciousness is the true suchness (*tathatā*) realized after the path; while true suchness is devoid of phenomena, the seeds of the fundamental activity of wisdom are all perfumed and perfected within the *ālayavijñāna*. Upon attaining the light of non-conceptual wisdom, it becomes the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

This would mean that the vehicle of principle (li-cheng) exists inherently and is subsequently attained as presently existing; that only after the realization of the Way can True Suchness (tathatā) transform sentient beings.
Is this not a vertical (sequential) interpretation?

If all three vehicles were entirely subsumed within the ālayavijñāna, this would be a horizontal (simultaneous) interpretation, and it would further conflate [the Buddhist view] with the primordial darkness from which consciousness arises [in certain non-Buddhist systems].
To be either diffuse or fragmented is to deviate from the true essence.
When the Original Tathāgata first appeared in the world, he intended to preach the reality directly;

however, for those who were not yet capable, he first employed the teaching of impermanence to dispel delusions, next used emptiness and purity to wash away attachments, and subsequently employed the method of sequential, distinct mental cultivation, only after which did he clarify the permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Nāgārjuna composed this treatise to expound upon this intention of the Buddha; by cleansing all attachments through the emptiness of non-apprehensibility and practicing in accordance with the emptiness of all phenomena, this is called being in correspondence with Prajñā.
Does this emptiness not itself empty ignorance?
If ignorance were empty, where would the seeds abide?
Having purified all phenomena, he points to emptiness to expound the Dharma, thereby establishing the characteristics of the four propositions.
These words are profound and subtle, yet they are without attachment or dwelling.
Just as one may take food only after an illness has been cured, and even that food is then digested,
how could the head emerge from the *ālayavijñāna* to give rise to all phenomena?
Fundamentally, because their views and pride have not been fully subdued, they seal themselves within these new texts, like adding water to long-standing ice.

Therefore, one should know that those treatises were not intended for sentient beings of the final age who are heavily burdened by attachments; rather, they are merely a single path of the Dharma for those outside the [ordinary] realms.
Furthermore, if the ālayavijñāna possesses all dharmas, how can it not possess the true suchness (tathatā) that follows the path?
If you say it does possess it, why then do you claim that true suchness is not the eighth consciousness?
I fear that this may still be a provisional teaching (*upāya*) extracted from within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
If one clings to it as a mere expedient, it will greatly obstruct the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
If it were indeed the ultimate reality, clinging to it would nonetheless constitute a dogmatic view (*dṛṣṭi*), like a child who consumes too much ghee and fears he will lose his life, and so forth.
If one can skillfully understand the intent behind refutation and establishment, one will be pure and free from obstruction regarding all sutras and treatises.
Fourth, to clarify the three dharmas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): the track of true nature (zhenxing gui) is taken as the essence of the vehicle.
That which is non-false is called "True," and that which is unchanging is called "Nature. This is the eternally abiding True Cause, the teacher of all Buddhas; it is this Dharma.
All sentient beings are likewise the One Vehicle; sentient beings are themselves the mark of Nirvana and cannot be extinguished further;
Nirvana is itself birth-and-death, characterized by neither extinction nor arising.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"This vehicle is neither moving nor emerging.
This refers precisely to this vehicle.

Regarding "contemplative observation" (guanzhao): it simply points to true nature, which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; this is contemplative observation, and it is precisely the emptiness of the primary meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā).

Regarding "provisional accomplishment" (zicheng): it simply points to the true nature as the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which contains and stores all conditioned phenomena and immeasurable requisites; this is the Tathāgatagarbha.

The three dharmas are neither identical nor different, just as when one discusses the light and the jewel within a mani-jewel: the light and the jewel are neither identical to the jewel nor different from it; they are neither vertical nor horizontal.
The three dharmas are likewise: they are both one and not one, and neither one nor not one; they are the inconceivable three dharmas.
If one is deluded regarding these three dharmas, one immediately incurs the three obstructions:
first, the dust-like afflictions within and beyond the realms obstruct the Tathāgatagarbha.
Second, the common and specific [afflictions] of view and thought obstruct the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Third, fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) obstructs the ultimate principle (*paramārtha-yukti*).
If the dust-like [afflictions] obstruct the realization of the infinite dharma-gates, then the "Aids and Accomplishments" (*pariniṣpanna-naya*) will be manifested.

If the hindrance of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) is immediately penetrated to reach the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha-śūnyatā), the track of contemplative observation (vipaśyanā-naya) becomes manifest.
If the hindrance of ignorance (avidyā) is immediately penetrated to reach the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the track of true nature (tathatā-naya) becomes manifest.
When the track of true nature (*dharmatā*) becomes manifest, it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
When contemplative observation becomes manifest, it is called Prajñā.
When the supportive accomplishment becomes manifest, it is called Liberation (*vimukti*).
These two constitute the adornment of concentration and wisdom, which adorn the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
The Dharma-body is the essence of the vehicle, while concentration and wisdom are its various requisites.
As the subsequent text states:
"His vehicle is high and broad, adorned with various jewels.

This is called the vehicle ridden by the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), which reaches *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), transcending the *tathatā* (suchness) beyond which no words can be spoken.
There are no words to be spoken, and likewise there should be no vehicle to be conveyed.
If one’s own practice has reached its completion, the meaning of the vehicle ceases;
if expedient transformation is not yet finished, the conveyance of others does not cease.
Therefore, the text says:
"The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna; according to the Dharma he has attained, adorned with the power of concentration and wisdom, he delivers sentient beings by means of this.
This is precisely its meaning.
For example, just as a charioteer is still called a "charioteer" even when the vehicle has reached its destination,
so too the vehicle of the fruit (phala-yāna) is still called a "vehicle" despite having completed its journey.
Furthermore, why must the term *yāna* be explained solely by the sense of "carrying" or "transporting"?
If one grasps the true nature, it neither moves nor emerges; thus, it is neither movement nor non-movement.
If one grasps contemplation and the supportive accomplishment, they can move and emerge; this is then called movement.
Movement and emergence are themselves non-movement and non-emergence;
this very non-movement and non-emergence is movement and emergence.
When discussing essence through its function, movement and emergence are non-movement and non-emergence.
To discuss function from the standpoint of essence, this very non-arising is itself arising.
Essence and function are non-dual, yet they appear as two.
For example:
Whether turning back or not turning back, all are *avaivartika*;
whether moving or unmoving, all are *vinaya*.
For this reason, both setting out and not setting out are called "vehicles," and so forth.

Third, regarding the clarification of the coarse and the sublime: within the three collections of the Tripiṭaka, there are meritorious deeds pertaining to the conditioned; these treatises take the three dharmas as the vehicle.
The four foundations of mindfulness constitute the wisdom derived from hearing; one mounts this vehicle of the teachings and proceeds to the four roots of goodness.
The four roots of goodness ride upon the vehicle of practice and reach the vision of the truths.
The vision of the truths rides upon the vehicle of realization and reaches the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Since these are provisional dharmas, once one has emerged from outside the triple world, one takes the ultimate truth as realization.
If one realizes [the truth], there is no movement and no perception of a real vehicle.
Alas, I reproach myself and wish to ask the World-Honored One: have I lost it, or have I not?
This is precisely that meaning.
The "half-syllables" (the provisional teachings) lead gradually forward but do not represent the ultimate meaning; therefore, the three dharmas therein are all coarse.
In the Shared Teaching, the wisdom of immediate emptiness takes the three dharmas as its skillful vehicle; the remaining intent is largely the same [as previously explained].

The stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) rides upon the vehicle of teaching; the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) rides upon the vehicle of practice; and the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) and the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*) ride upon the vehicle of realization.
This is also a partial explanation, and is therefore considered coarse.

In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the supportive practice (zicheng) serves to support contemplative insight (guanzhao), and contemplative insight opens up true nature (zhenxing); thus, these three dharmas constitute the vehicle.

The ten stages of faith (shixin) are the vehicle of teaching; the ten abidings (shizhu) are the vehicle of practice; and the ten grounds (shidi) are the vehicle of realization, culminating in dwelling within the *sarvajñā* of wondrous enlightenment.
The conditions, once completed through cultivation, immediately pass away; only true cultivation remains.
If this is so, then the supportive cultivation comes first, contemplative illumination follows next, and true nature comes last.

These three are distinct in their vertical differentiation; even if they were not Mahāyāna, these three would still be different from it. They are not Mahāyāna in their horizontal arrangement; they are merely expedient methods, and for this reason, they are considered coarse.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the pointing toward the true mark (shixiang) as the emptiness of the primary meaning (diyiyi kong) is termed "vertical" (zong).
Since the emptiness of the primary meaning is itself the true mark, and the true mark is not vertical, how could this emptiness be vertical?
To point to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as the Tathāgatagarbha is termed "horizontal" (transverse).
Since the Tathāgatagarbha is itself the true mark, and the true mark is not horizontal, how could this treasury be horizontal?
Therefore, it cannot be contemplated vertically nor can it be contemplated horizontally; thus it is called the "inconceivable dharma," which is precisely what is meant by "wondrous.

To take emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the *dharmadhātu* as the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), while emptiness is vertical and the *dharmadhātu* is horizontal—how could the true mark not be both vertical and horizontal?
If you point to emptiness as the Tathāgatagarbha, since emptiness is not horizontal, how could the Garbha be horizontal?
If you point to the Tathāgatagarbha as emptiness, since the Garbha is not vertical, how could emptiness be vertical?

Taking the true reality as emptiness and the treasury, the true reality is neither vertical nor horizontal, and emptiness and the treasury are likewise neither vertical nor horizontal; they are interpenetrating and mutually identical in an inconceivable manner, and for this reason it is called "wondrous."
Taking the *tathāgatagarbha* as its breadth and taking the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) as its height, it is therefore said that the chariot is high and broad.
Since the *tathāgatagarbha* is the true mark (*dharmatā*), the chariot is not [merely] broad.
The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); therefore, its carriage is not high.
Since the true mark itself is emptiness, how could it not be high?
Since the true mark itself is the Tathāgatagarbha, how could it not be vast?
Furthermore, because the marked ultimate reality (lakṣaṇa) is the Tathāgatagarbha, it is said to be adorned with many jewels and attended by numerous servants.

Because the marked ultimate reality is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā), it is said that there is a great white ox—plump, strong, and powerful, whose gait is level and upright, swift as the wind; its wisdom is untainted, and thus it is called "white."
It is called "possessing great power" because it can destroy delusions.
Middle-way wisdom is called "level and upright.
Because it enters the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*), its swiftness is like the wind.
The three inconceivable dharmas together constitute the Great Vehicle; how could there be any distinction between vertical and horizontal, or between the individual and the collective?
Such a vehicle of teaching is neither vertical nor horizontal; that which the five stages of practice ride upon leads to the stage of semblance-understanding.
This vehicle of practice is neither longitudinal nor transverse; resembling the understanding of what is to be mounted, it reaches the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

This vehicle of realization is neither longitudinal nor transverse; that which is mounted upon by the ten stages reaches the abiding within the *sarvajñā* of wondrous enlightenment; therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Vehicle."
It is further said:
"This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, the foremost in purity.
Thus, when the lecture was established at Waguan Temple, people dreamed of those who listened to it departing through the gate riding upon this very vehicle.
A lecture hall was established there, and people dreamed that yellow-clad figures filled the roads.
Judging by these signs, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox became clear!
If one were to categorize these coarse and subtle vehicles according to the five flavors, the milk-teaching consists of one coarse and one subtle aspect.
Curd is one coarse [teaching].
Fresh butter has three coarse and one subtle [teachings].
Refined butter has two coarse and one subtle [teachings].
All other sutras employ various vertical and horizontal skillful means to explain the reality that is neither vertical nor horizontal; therefore, they are said to be "coarse.
This present sutra, however, directly abandons such skillful means and thus adds to it the quality of being "sublime," and so forth.
Fourth, "revealing the coarse to manifest the subtle" refers to the three phrases from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states:
"Buddha-nature is also one," because all sentient beings are entirely of the One Vehicle.
This is the single vehicle (ekayāna) that is immovable and non-emergent; therefore, it is fully endowed with the three dharmas, neither vertical nor horizontal.
Indeed, all who possess a mind are complete with this principle, yet within their families, from the eldest to the youngest, none at all realize it; for this reason, it is considered coarse.
Now, for the sake of all sentient beings, I reveal the precious treasury of awakening; I weed out the weeds and filth to uncover the gold within the storehouse.
All those who are free from hindrance shall transcend birth and death by means of this single path.
If one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle; there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, and for this reason it is wondrous.
The Sūtra says:
"The Buddha-nature is neither one nor not one."
Because the categories of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are not fixed.

If one clings to the notion that wisdom cultivated through conditions can definitively manifest the principle, yet that wisdom itself is not the principle, then its illuminating function will lack clarity; one will fail to see the Buddha-nature, and for this reason, such a view is considered coarse.

Now, the wisdom that opens up fixed attachments is itself non-fixed wisdom; it is principle within wisdom and wisdom within principle. It does not cling to numbers, such as "three" or "one," nor does it cling to non-numbers, being neither three nor one. This is what is called the wondrous wisdom of non-attachment.
It is able to shatter all determinate characteristics as well as indeterminate characteristics, yet there is neither that which shatters nor that which is shattered.

Like a Wheel-Turning King who can both destroy and establish, like the sun that dispels darkness and brings forth things, or like a physician who removes the film from a pearl to nourish it—this is precisely the wondrous wisdom of the Mahāyāna, neither vertical nor horizontal.
The Sūtra states:
"Buddha-nature is also not one," because it speaks of the three vehicles.
This refers to the various provisional vehicles, such as the three vehicles, the five vehicles, and the seven vehicles.

If one abides in the various vehicles, these are merely mundane virtues and the partial truth; because they involve entry through the gates of sensory perception and are proximate, they are considered coarse.
Now, if one definitively realizes that all vehicles are themselves the Tathāgatagarbha—the name "garbha" signifying Buddha-nature—[then one has attained the subtle].
From the wholesome states of humans and devas up to the other vehicles, none move from the fundamental Dharma; this is precisely what is "wondrous.
One should know that these three phrases encompass all phenomena; there is nothing that is not Buddha-nature, and all are entirely wondrous.
Since there is no coarse [phenomenon] to be depended upon, it is the wondrousness that transcends all dependence.

Fifth, clarifying the beginning and end: one does not take the five grades of the Dharma-vehicle as the beginning; rather, one takes the single thought-moment of the ordinary person’s stage, which possesses the ten dharma-realms and ten kinds of characteristics and natures, as the beginning of the three dharmas.
What are they? These ten kinds of characteristics and natures are simply the three tracks.
Thus, their essence is the track of true nature;
Suchness (tathatā) as nature refers to the internal; it is the track of contemplative insight (prajñā).
Suchness as characteristic refers to the external; it is merit (puṇya), which is the track of supportive accomplishment (sambhāra).
Power (*bala*) is the cause of realization (*vyañjana-hetu*), which is the mode of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*);
action (*karman*) is the diligent cultivation of the myriad practices, which constitutes the supportive cause (*parigraha-hetu*);
and the causal factor (*hetu*) is the causal condition of habituation (*abhyāsa-hetu*), which belongs to contemplative observation.
The "condition" (pratyaya) refers to the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), which belongs to the category of the supporting-accomplishing [wisdom];

the "fruit" (phala) refers to the fruit of cultivation (abhyāsa-phala), which belongs to the category of the observing-reflecting [wisdom]; and the "retribution" (vipāka) refers to the retribution of cultivation (abhyāsa-vipāka), which belongs to the category of the supporting-accomplishing [wisdom].
Regarding "the beginning and the end being equal": emptiness and so forth constitute contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*);
the provisional and so forth constitute supportive accomplishment (*sambhāra*);
and the middle constitutes true nature (*dharmatā*).
To proceed directly to the discussion of the three modes (*triyāna*) based on the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) within a single realm:

here we clarify that within a single thought-moment of an ordinary mind, all ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātus*) are fully present; in each and every realm, there are the nature and characteristics of afflictions, the nature and characteristics of evil karma, and the nature and characteristics of the path of suffering.
If there is the nature and characteristic of ignorance and afflictions, this is itself the nature and characteristic of the wisdom of contemplative observation. Why?
Because ignorance arises by being deluded regarding clarity.
If one understands ignorance, that itself is clarity.
As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When ignorance is transformed, it changes into clarity."
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself clarity (*vidyā*).
One should know that clarity does not exist apart from ignorance; it is like ice being water, and water being ice.

Furthermore, the mind of an ordinary person in a single thought-moment possesses all ten realms, each fully containing the nature and characteristics of evil karma. Indeed, the very nature and characteristics of evil are identical to the nature and characteristics of goodness; because goodness exists through evil, there is no goodness apart from evil. By overturning these various evils, they are immediately transformed into the resources that perfect goodness.

Just as fire-nature exists within bamboo, yet it is not yet the actual phenomenon of fire, and thus, though present, does not burn; when it encounters conditions and becomes a phenomenon, it can then burn objects.
Evil is likewise the nature of good; it is not yet the actual phenomenon.
When meeting with conditions, one can accomplish matters and thereby overturn evil.
It is like bamboo containing fire: once the fire emerges, it burns the bamboo itself.
Within evil there is good; when the good is accomplished, it in turn destroys the evil.
Therefore, the very characteristic of an evil nature is itself the characteristic of a virtuous nature.

In every single thought-moment of an ordinary person, there exist the characteristics of the ten realms of consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth, which constitute the nature of the path of suffering.
To be deluded regarding this path of suffering is to wander aimlessly through the vast expanse of birth and death; this is to mistake the Dharma-body for the path of suffering.
There is no Dharma-body apart from the path of suffering, just as when one mistakes south for north, there is no separate "south" that exists elsewhere.
If one awakens to birth and death, it is precisely the Dharma-body; therefore it is said:
"The nature and characteristics of the path of suffering are themselves the nature and characteristics of the Dharma-body.
Indeed, all who possess a mind have the nature and characteristics of the three paths, which are themselves the nature and characteristics of the three tracks (trivartman).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"The host of afflictions constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata.
This is precisely what that means.
If one says that such power and such agency constitute the arousal of the bodhicitta, this is the initial stirring of true nature (tathatā).
Such causes are the initial stirring of contemplative observation (vipaśyanā).
Such conditions are that which support and bring about the initial stirring [of awakening].
Such fruits arise because, through contemplative observation of this stirring, one establishes the causal habituation and thereby realizes the fulfillment of the habitual fruit of prajñā.
Regarding such retribution: because the causal conditions that bring about its manifestation serve as the contributory causes, one attains the fulfillment of the fruit of liberation.
Since the fruit of retribution is fulfilled, the Dharma-body is likewise fulfilled; this constitutes the ultimate fulfillment of the three virtues, which is named the Secret Treasury.
Regarding the equality of the fundamental and the derivative: the three tracks of the nature-virtue (xingde) lie in profound latency, neither vertical nor horizontal;
the three tracks of the cultivation-virtue (xiude) manifest in clarity, neither vertical nor horizontal.
It is called "equality" because it is equal in its hiddenness, equal in its enumeration, and equal in its excellence;
it is also manifestly equal in its hiddenness, equal in its enumeration, and equal in its excellence.
Furthermore, it refers to the equality of emptiness, the equality of the provisional, and the equality of the Middle Way, and so forth.
Sixth, regarding the "categorical penetration of the three dharmas": previously, by means of the dharma of the three tracks from beginning to end, there was vertical penetration without obstruction.
Now, desiring horizontal penetration of all dharmas so that they are entirely unobstructed, one categorically penetrates these various sets of three dharmas.

Why is this? While the names differ according to the conditions they address, their essential meaning is the same. These ten general categories provide a broad understanding; the remaining points may be inferred.

They are: the three paths, the three consciousnesses, the three Buddha-natures, the three prajñās, the three enlightenments, the three Great Vehicles, the three bodies, the three nirvāṇas, the three jewels, and the three virtues.
Although there are immeasurable triads of dharmas, only ten are employed here; this is done to present the essential points and clarify the beginning and end [of the path].
The three paths of saṃsāra are the fundamental nature of birth and death, and therefore they constitute the beginning.

If one wishes to go against the current of birth and death, one must understand the three consciousnesses, know the three Buddha-natures, give rise to the three wisdoms, generate the three bodhicittas, practice the three Mahāyānas, realize the three bodies, and achieve the three nirvāṇas. These are the Three Jewels, which benefit all beings; when the conditions for transformation are exhausted, one enters the three virtues and abides in the secret treasury, and so forth.
First, regarding the universal application across the three paths:
the track of true nature (*dharmatā-naya*) is the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*);
the track of contemplative observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-naya*) is the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
If the "track of accomplishment" (*sambhāra-mārga*) is the path of action (*karmapatha*),
and the "track of suffering" (*duḥkha-mārga*) is the true nature (*dharmatā*),

does this not mean that what is described in the subsequent text as "the marks of the world are eternally abiding" is precisely that very birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?

Afflictions are themselves contemplation; contemplation fundamentally illuminates delusion. Where there is no delusion, there is no illumination; this is precisely what is meant by the emptiness of all phenomena.
As the text says:
"All phenomena, from the very beginning, have always been characterized by quiescent extinction."
"Afflictions themselves are the contemplative observation.
This illumination is like fire arising from fuel.
As the text says:
"Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, if there were those who heard even a single phrase, they have all already attained the Way of the Buddha.
It further says:
"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, they illuminate the ten directions everywhere."
This is precisely hearing and realizing the sublime phrase regarding the essence of afflictions.
As for "the completion of resources being the path of karma," evil is the resource for good; without evil, there is also no good.
The text says:
"When evil spirits enter our hearts and revile and insult us, we shall endure these matters because we practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

It further states that if evil does not come upon one to inflict harm, there is no occasion for the application of mindfulness; the application of mindfulness arises precisely because of the infliction of evil, and so forth.

Furthermore, among the assembly of those who followed the Dharma under the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, there were some who heard the words of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging and reviled, abused, and struck him;
yet due to their own past evil karma, they encountered Never-Disparaging once more, and through his teaching and transformation, they all attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Devadatta is a spiritual friend; is it not the case that evil serves as his support?
The three modes of conduct are the three paths; this constitutes the principle of nature. By practicing what is not the path, one attains penetration into the Buddha-way.
In the five stages, one practices the non-path through contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and thereby penetrates the Buddha-way.
In the stage of the purification of the six sense organs, one practices the non-path in a semblance manner and thereby penetrates the Buddha-way.
The Ten Abodes depart from [delusion] and immediately practice the true and partial realization upon the non-path, thereby attaining penetration into the Buddha-way.
At the stage of Subtle Enlightenment, one ultimately practices upon the non-path, thereby attaining penetration into the Buddha-way, and so forth.
Second, regarding the universal application across the three consciousnesses: the *amala-vijñāna* is the track of true nature (*zhenxing gui*);
